p.title: A Systematic Review and Analysis of Intelligence-Based Pathfinding Algorithms in the Field of Video Games

ext.title: A Systematic Review and Analysis of Intelligence-Based Pathfinding Algorithms in the Field of Video Games
ext.venue: Applied Sciences 12(11), 5499 (MDPI). Received 25 Mar 2022; accepted 24 May 2022; published 28 May 2022.
ext.document_type: Journal article (open access, CC BY). Titled a systematic review, but the body is a single-environment benchmark of four pathfinding algorithms plus a descriptive literature comparison. No review protocol (databases, search strings, inclusion rules, paper counts) is reported.
ext.coverage: Full text read: the entire extracted text file (1,811 lines, journal pages 1-30 including references 1-95), in chunks of about 400 lines. Annotation file read in full: 68 entries (67 highlights, 1 free-text note). Metadata hint confirmed against the PDF header; authors' full names added. No parts skipped.
ext.identification: None. Descriptive benchmark: the same grids are fed to each algorithm and the outputs are ranked. There is no causal design, no controls for hardware or run-to-run variance, and no repeated trials. Theory section is a taxonomy (uninformed / informed-heuristic / metaheuristic), not a tested hypothesis.
ext.theory: Taxonomy only. Pathfinding is split into uninformed (BFS, Dijkstra), informed/heuristic (A*, Greedy Best First, D* Lite, HPA*, JPS) and metaheuristic (GA, ACO) families, and static vs dynamic. The paper argues heuristic methods save time by pruning the search space (Sections 2, 3.2). No formal model is stated beyond the cost functions F(n)=G(n)+H(n) and the Table 2 complexity expressions.
ext.research_question: Which of four pathfinding algorithms (Dijkstra, A*, Breadth First Search, Greedy Best First) performs best on 2D square grids of size 4x4 to 32x32, with and without obstacles, in terms of execution time, total iteration blocks, computed blocks and shortest path length, so that game developers can choose one? Secondary: how do the families compare in the literature on memory and time (Table 5).
ext.data: Synthetic game-style grids generated in the Unity engine: 2D square (octile) grids of 4x4, 8x8, 16x16 and 32x32 cells, each run with and without obstacles. Unit = one algorithm run on one grid configuration. Reported cells: 4 algorithms x 4 sizes x 2 conditions = 32 algorithm-by-grid results (16 rows in each of Tables 3 and 4). Not reported: number of repetitions, start and goal placement, obstacle layout or density, the iteration count k, hardware, and run dates. Literature input for Section 3 and Table 5: 95 references, span 1959 to 2022 (count of papers actually screened not stated). No real-world dataset.
ext.method: Implemented BFS, Dijkstra, A* and Greedy Best First in Unity (Algorithms 1-4; the "GRIN_PF" Algorithm 6 is a harness that loops over these four). Per run recorded: total iteration blocks, total computed blocks excluding the shortest path, execution time in ms, and shortest path length in blocks (Section 5, p.19-20). Results compared as within-size rankings and narrative (Section 6, p.23-26). Theoretical side: asymptotic time/space table (Table 2, p.14) and a pairwise literature comparison table with category, time, memory, implemented yes/no, and cited source (Table 5, p.26-27). No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or repeated timings. Memory was not measured.
ext.scope: Population: single-agent pathfinding on regular 2D square grids in a game-style environment. Dynamic obstacles and 3D, hexagonal, triangular or irregular (waypoint, visibility graph, navmesh) grids are discussed but not tested. Institutions: VIT Chennai (India) and Universiti Teknologi PETRONAS (Malaysia); funded by YUTP grant 015LC0-134. Era: article 2022; cited literature 1959-2022. Not related to lobbying, elections, legislators, persuasion/turnout or text measurement.

key_findings.finding: Without obstacles, Greedy Best First is fastest at every grid size; Dijkstra is slowest at every size.
key_findings.location: Section 6, p.23-24; Table 3 p.20-21; Figure 15 p.24

key_findings.finding: The Dijkstra-to-GBF time gap widens with grid size (computed from Table 3 values, not stated by the authors).
Without obstacles, GBF returns the same shortest path length as the other three algorithms at every size, yet the text calls GBF 'not optimal'. The open-grid table shows no length penalty.
key_findings.location: Table 3 p.20-21; text p.24 and p.25-26
key_findings.numbers: Shortest path length (blocks) for all four algorithms: 5, 13, 29, 61 for 4x4, 8x8, 16x16, 32x32

key_findings.finding: GBF expands almost no nodes without obstacles; BFS and Dijkstra have identical iteration counts at every open-grid size.
key_findings.numbers: Computed blocks without SPL, GBF: 1, 1, 1, 1. Dijkstra: 9, 49, 225, 961. BFS: 9, 49, 225, 961. Total iterations for Dijkstra and BFS both 14, 62, 254, 1022

key_findings.finding: Dijkstra and BFS execution times differ by only 0.7% to 15% despite identical iteration counts; no repeated trials are reported, so these gaps cannot be separated from timing noise.
key_findings.location: Table 3 p.20-21 (reviewer computation); text p.23-24 says 'almost similar'

key_findings.finding: With obstacles, GBF is fastest at 8x8, 16x16 and 32x32; A* is fastest at 4x4, where all four are within about 2 ms.

With obstacles, GBF path length is longer at 16x16 and 32x32, but shorter than the optimal-family result at 8x8; the 8x8 result is not discussed and is inconsistent with Dijkstra and A* returning optimal lengths on unit-cost grids.
key_findings.numbers: Shortest path length: 8x8 GBF 13 vs Dijkstra/A*/BFS 15; 16x16 GBF 37 vs 31; 32x32 GBF 81 vs 75

key_findings.finding: With obstacles, A* expands fewer nodes than Dijkstra at 16x16 and 32x32 but more at 8x8.
key_findings.numbers: Total iterations A* vs Dijkstra: 8x8 32 vs 30; 16x16 140 vs 177; 32x32 587 vs 754

key_findings.finding: The memory conclusions in Section 6 and Table 5 are not measured. Memory is inferred from computed-block counts or taken from cited literature. Section 5 lists the measured parameters and memory is not among them.
key_findings.location: Section 5 p.19-20; Section 6 p.24-26; Table 5 p.26-27
key_findings.numbers: Measured: iterations, computed blocks, time (ms), path length. Memory: none

key_findings.finding: The headline ranking (GBF fastest and least memory; A* second; BFS third; Dijkstra worst, with 'on average' used without weighting) rests on one run per cell.
key_findings.numbers: Single run per algorithm-grid cell reported in Tables 3-4

key_findings.finding: Table 5 cites sources whose reference-list entries do not match the claims. Examples: the D* Lite vs A* memory claim cites [93] (a 2017 ambulance-routing paper) but gives 2009; BFS vs DFS cites [90] (a 2022 healthcare Q-learning paper); Dijkstra vs GA cites [91] (a 2021 Mars-landing paper). The text dates A* to 1986 but cites [38], a 1968 IEEE paper.
key_findings.location: Table 5 p.26-27; Section 3.2.1 p.11; reference list p.28-30
key_findings.numbers: Refs [90]-[95] are not about pathfinding (healthcare, Mars landing, UAV, ambulance routing, metabolic pathfinding, vehicle routing)

key_findings.finding: The 'GRIN_PF outperforms existing approaches' claim is not tested. Algorithm 6 is a loop running the four existing algorithms; no GRIN_PF-specific result appears in Sections 5-6.
key_findings.numbers: No GRIN_PF timing or path numbers in any table or figure

key_findings.finding: Authors' remark on the open problem: dynamic obstacles and realistic movement remain unsolved; they suggest sensor-equipped agents and runtime algorithm switching, without testing either.
key_findings.location: Section 6 p.26 (pre-processing and splines); Conclusion p.27

limitations: Stated by authors: dynamic obstacles would need 'much effort' to handle reactively (Conclusion, p.27); the study uses a 2D square grid only (Abstract; Section 2.1, p.4); the authors say GBF is 'not optimal' (p.24, p.26); realism of movement and pre-processing issues are discussed (p.26) but not tested.
Observed: no repetitions, variance, or timing protocol; hardware and Unity version unreported; start/goal placement, obstacle layout and density, and iteration count k are not specified.
Observed: memory is never measured, though Section 6 and Table 5 rank algorithms by memory.
Observed: the 'systematic review' has no reported search protocol, databases, inclusion or exclusion criteria, or paper counts.
Observed: Table 5 mixes implemented comparisons with literature-derived comparisons and cites sources that do not match the claims (see key findings).
Observed: GRIN_PF is presented as the proposed method, but it is only a harness; the conclusion's claim that it outperforms existing approaches is untested.
Observed: the 8x8 with-obstacle path-length anomaly (GBF 13 vs optimal-family 15) is unexplained, which raises a question about how path length is counted.
measures: Execution time (ms) per algorithm per grid
Total computed blocks without shortest path length
Asymptotic time T(n) and space S(n) (Table 2)
Memory usage: claimed in Table 5 and Section 6, not measured

rel.summary_md:
Lawande et al. (2022) call the paper a systematic review, but it is really a benchmark of four algorithms on one setup: BFS, Dijkstra, A* and Greedy Best First (GBF), each run once on Unity square grids from 4x4 to 32x32, with and without obstacles. It reports no search protocol, no repeated trials, no hardware details and no measured memory, so its memory rankings and the Table 5 citations (several of which do not match the claims) cannot be relied on. The usable results are narrow. With no obstacles, GBF is fastest at every size; Dijkstra is 2.8x to 21.6x slower than GBF, and all four find the same path length. With obstacles, GBF stays fastest from 8x8 up, but its paths get longer (37 vs 31 at 16x16, 81 vs 75 at 32x32). A* expands fewer nodes than Dijkstra on the larger grids (587 vs 754 iterations at 32x32) and still returns the optimal length. D* and D* Lite are only described, never tested. The proposed GRIN_PF is just a loop that runs the four existing algorithms.

What this means for the system as built is mostly a check on design choices, not new evidence. The one sharp bearing comes from the paper's GBF-with-obstacles result. The dashboard's recruitment path first runs an exact max-product Dijkstra backward from the target (`distToTarget`), then walks forward greedily, choosing at each hop the neighbour with the highest edge probability times its precomputed reliability to the target. That walk is optimal only while the precomputed reliabilities are exact. Once a user drops members, the walk skips them but the reliabilities are still computed through them. The walk then becomes a greedy best-first search on an out-of-date estimate, which is the case where the paper shows longer, non-optimal paths. Terrier's walk router already does textbook A* with an admissible straight-line estimate, which is the setting where the paper's A* result applies best. For the non-spatial social graphs, the paper offers no usable heuristic.

bearings.paper_claim: With obstacles, the greedy method (GBF) is fastest but returns longer, non-optimal paths: 37 vs 31 blocks at 16x16 and 81 vs 75 at 32x32. With no obstacles it matches the optimal length (5/13/29/61). A greedy walk is optimal only when its estimate is exact for the graph actually being searched.
bearings.paper_location: Table 3 p.20-21; Table 4 p.22-23; Section 6 p.24-26
bearings.system_side: distToTarget runs an exact max-product Dijkstra from the target over the full PE graph and does not exclude dropped members. tracePath then walks forward greedily by argmax PE[cur][v]*dT[v] and skips dropped and already-seen nodes. With no drops, this greedy descent on an exact estimate is optimal. With drops, dT still counts routes through the excluded members, so the walk becomes a greedy best-first search on an out-of-date estimate. It can return a less reliable chain, or 'unreachable' when a route exists. bestSponsors reuses the same dT. The code comment at line 735 still says 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL'. This is a single-path code reading (UNVERIFIED per DE-062).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the algorithmic point carries over, that greedy search on an inexact estimate loses optimality once obstacles are present. The grid timings do not. The graph has N=533 nodes and recomputing dT is O(N^2), about 0.3M operations, so the cheap remedy is to exclude dropped members in distToTarget, not incremental replanning. Must be reproduced by a second path, such as a test case that drops a bridging member, before any claim is made.

bearings.paper_claim: On larger grids, A* expands fewer nodes than Dijkstra and returns the same optimal path length (iterations 140 vs 177 at 16x16 and 587 vs 754 at 32x32, with obstacles). The exception is 8x8, where A* expands more (32 vs 30). Execution times are 3975 vs 5678 ms at 32x32, single run.
bearings.system_side: Terrier's deadhead router is A* over the noded TIGER street graph. Its estimate is the straight-line distance to the nearest goal minus NODE_SLACK_M, floored at 0. It falls back to h=0 (plain Dijkstra) when any goal lacks coordinates, so the estimate stays admissible and the result optimal.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is the closest match in the system, a spatial graph with a metric estimate. Road networks are not uniform grids, the paper's figures are single runs with unreported hardware, and its gains appear only from 16x16 up. The paper supports the design choice (an admissible A* estimate is a free speedup that keeps optimality). It does not give a measured speedup for street networks.

bearings.paper_claim: Informed (A*) search cuts expansions only through an estimate H(n) of remaining cost. On grids that estimate is geometric. Without one, A* reduces to Dijkstra (H=0 is how the paper derives Dijkstra from A*).
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.1.2 p.9-10 (H(n)=0 for Dijkstra); Section 3.2.1 p.11; Table 4 p.22-23
bearings.system_side: The staffer router is bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0, plus Yen loopless alternatives and exact tie-breaking. The default search is one-directional to a virtual sink. The metadata records heuristic 0 explicitly.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The staffer graph has no spatial embedding, so the paper's Euclidean/octile estimates do not apply. The A* gain from the paper carries over only if an admissible estimate is built for a non-metric graph, such as ALT landmark bounds, which is deferred (per memory). The paper does not test that. It supports the decision to keep h=0 until such an estimate exists. It does not support adding A* by name.

bearings.paper_claim: GBF picks the locally best option at each step ('always try to pick the best track at that particular moment'). It is the fastest of the four but makes no optimality claim. D* and D* Lite (dynamic replanning) are described in Section 3.2.3 but not implemented or tested.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.2.2 p.12; Section 3.2.3 p.12-13; Table 4 p.22-23
bearings.system_side: build_route is a greedy best-first construction. A heap orders candidate edges by (gain - lambda(1-p))/cost, with a K=5 out-degree cap. It is not an optimal search. The system instead takes non-dominated points across five lambda values. There is no incremental replanning (MOPBD* is concept only).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only by analogy: the route finder solves a budgeted coverage problem, not a point-to-point shortest path, so the paper's path-length results do not transfer. The paper gives no evidence on D* Lite performance, so it cannot justify building the replanning layer that Paul marked 'Very interesting'.

gaps_exposed: The dashboard recruitment path (distToTarget at make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:734) computes target reliabilities without excluding dropped members, while tracePath (line 740) skips them. With drops, the 'provably optimal' chain becomes a greedy walk on an out-of-date estimate. No test covers the case where a dropped member was on the route. Single-path observation, UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

There is no admissible estimate for the non-spatial social graphs (cosponsor, staffer), so A*-family speedups are not available there. ALT landmarks remain deferred. The paper's grid heuristics do not fill this gap.

No component replans incrementally (D*/D* Lite/LPA*) when the graph changes. For N=533 a full recompute is cheap enough. It would matter only for the multi-million-pair staffer graph, and the paper gives no evidence on that.
flags: The paper's memory rankings (GBF 'least memory', Dijkstra 'most memory usage') were never measured. Section 5 lists no memory metric. Do not cite this paper for memory claims.

The paper is not a systematic review (no protocol, databases or counts), and Table 5 cites references [90]-[95] that do not support the claims attached to them. Cite only the Table 3-4 counts, and label them single-run.
The GRIN_PF 'outperforms existing approaches' claim is untested. Do not cite it.

Wording: the dashboard comment calls the chain 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL ... mathematical certainty ... exact, maximal probability' (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:735-737). That holds only for the modeled kernel with no drops, and chainHold is a modeled output that depends on ASKM, not an empirical probability (D-025 spirit). The UI tooltip at line 1119 is already correctly hedged.
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, and says nothing about LDA or reciprocity. No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul files this paper in his Path-Finding folder as a citation only, with no takeaways. His only mark is the free-text note 'Very interesting' beside the D* node-state passage. The component positions also cite it as grounding for D*/D* Lite replanning (cosponsor-route-pareto) and as indirect support for Terrier's street routing. The evidence only partly supports that reading. The paper describes D* but never runs it, so it cannot ground the replanning layer Paul names in his addendum. Its tested contribution is narrower: A* beats Dijkstra on node expansions on larger grids when it has an admissible geometric estimate, and greedy search loses optimality once obstacles appear. Paul's note is not stale, since the system still has no incremental replanning. But the paper points somewhere more practical than D* Lite: the 533-node dashboard path should simply recompute its exact backward pass once members are dropped. His 'A* heuristics that cope with unstable information' goal (Rongkuan, Oropeza-Martinez) gets nothing from this paper for non-spatial graphs. The only place its A* evidence applies cleanly is Terrier's street router, which already uses an admissible straight-line estimate.

related.why: Chen 2016 grounds the max-product (most-reliable) objective that the dashboard path optimizes. Lawande supplies the greedy-vs-exact search contrast that shows where that path loses optimality once nodes are dropped.
Both address the cost of single-source shortest paths. Duan gives asymptotic improvements over Dijkstra on directed graphs, while Lawande gives only single-run grid timings.
MOPBD* is the multi-objective D* Lite that the cosponsor route cites as concept. Lawande describes the D* family but tests none of it.
An improved D* Lite tested on a grid with dynamic obstacles, which Lawande leaves untested.
Another D* Lite variant with dynamic replanning results, filling the replanning-evidence gap that Lawande only discusses.
Multi-agent CBS with D* Lite replanning, which extends past Lawande's single-agent static-grid scope.
Applies shortest-path algorithms to social-network tie strengths, the non-spatial setting where Lawande's grid heuristics do not carry over.
